script.opening: "This is awkward, doctor. The end of my penis keeps getting red, sore and itchy under the foreskin, with a bit of discharge — it’s happened a few times over the last few months. And now the foreskin’s getting tight and hard to pull back. Can you sort it?"

facts.text: Three or four episodes over 6 months, each lasting a week or two. Red, sore, itchy, a bit wet under the foreskin, sometimes white cheesy stuff. No lumps or ulcers he has noticed. Used some thrush cream from the chemist once — it helped a bit.

Tighter over the last 2 months; can only pull it back halfway now. Hasn’t got stuck behind the head. If asked: noticed the skin at the tip "looks a bit whiter and shiny". Stream OK, no spraying, no pain passing urine.
Washes "thoroughly" with shower gel twice a day. No new condoms or creams.
"Not that I’ve noticed." Hasn’t had a blood test for years. Doesn’t know about diabetes in the family — "we never talked about health".
Married 25 years, wife is his only partner. No discharge from the urethra. Wife has had thrush "now and then".
Overweight (BMI about 31). High blood pressure — takes amlodipine. No allergies. Drives a taxi. Smokes 10 a day.

Embarrassed, uses vague words ("down there"). Relax if the doctor is matter-of-fact. Surprised by the diabetes link: "Diabetes? I’d not thought of that." Prefer to send a photo or be examined at the surgery rather than show it on video.

ice.ideas: "An infection — thrush, maybe. Some cream should sort it."
ice.concerns: "With the tightness, I’m worried it’s something serious — cancer, even." Also worried about sex with his wife.
ice.expectations: "A cream that clears it for good."

cues: "It keeps coming back" — recurrence points to an underlying cause such as diabetes.
"The foreskin’s getting tight" — possible lichen sclerosus or pathological phimosis.
"I haven’t had a blood test for years" (if asked about check-ups) — opportunity to test for diabetes.

checkpoints.text: Recognises BALANITIS (± balanoposthitis) and developing PHIMOSIS (non-retractile foreskin) from the recurrent sore/itchy glans and increasing retraction difficulty, examining face to face with consent and a chaperone offered, without forcible retraction
Checks GLUCOSE/HbA1c — recognising recurrent candidal balanitis’s strong link with (and possible presentation of) DIABETES

Screens the CAUSES (BASHH 2025: irritant dermatitis and dermatoses common, Candida a minority) — irritant/contact dermatitis and hygiene, candidal/infective, bacterial/STI (GUM if at risk), psoriasis/lichen planus, and lichen sclerosus/BXO
Recognises LICHEN SCLEROSUS (BXO) — white scarring causing pathological phimosis/meatal stenosis with a small penile SCC risk — needing dermatology/urology referral

Manages per cause (hygiene advice, topical antifungal ± steroid/antibacterial, treat diabetes) and REFERS for pathological phimosis, suspected BXO, recurrent/refractory disease or a suspicious lesion (NICE NG12) — never forcibly retracting, and treating paraphimosis as a same-day emergency
Handles an embarrassing problem sensitively, reassures and explains the diagnosis/cause, and checks understanding
Communicates the diabetes check and referral reasoning clearly without alarming

Safety-nets and follows up: glucose result, response to treatment, referral for phimosis/BXO/refractory or suspicious lesions, hygiene advice, and review — cause-directed care + diabetes check + appropriate referral

worked.txt: "There’s no need to be embarrassed — this is common and we’ll sort it. I’d like to examine you in person — you’re welcome to have a chaperone — gently, and I won’t force the foreskin back. The redness and soreness is balanitis, and the tightening you describe is the foreskin becoming harder to retract."

"Because it keeps coming back, I want to check your blood sugar — recurrent soreness like this can be linked to diabetes, and occasionally it’s the first sign. So a glucose/HbA1c test is important here."

"Irritation from soaps or washing, and skin conditions, are common causes; a thrush (yeast) infection is one possible cause, which responds to an antifungal cream, sometimes with a mild steroid. Everyone benefits from gentle hygiene — wash with water, use a moisturiser instead of soap, and dry well. If there’s any STI risk we can screen for that too."

"One thing I’m checking for is a skin condition called lichen sclerosus, which causes whitish scarring and tightening — if that’s what’s tightening your foreskin, it needs a specialist, and sometimes a steroid ointment or a circumcision."
"If the foreskin stays tight, it looks scarred, or it keeps recurring despite treatment, I’ll refer you to urology. Please don’t force the foreskin back, as that can cause harm."

"If the foreskin ever gets stuck back and won’t go forward, go to A&E the same day. Come back if it’s not settling, the foreskin won’t move, or you notice any persistent lump, white patch or non-healing sore — that I’d want looked at promptly."

f.learning: BALANITIS is inflammation of the glans (balanoposthitis if the foreskin is also involved), presenting as a red, sore, itchy glans with discharge; recurrent episodes and progressive difficulty retracting the foreskin suggest developing PHIMOSIS (non-retractile foreskin) — examine without forcibly retracting. Irritant or contact dermatitis and dermatoses are common causes and Candida is a minority cause (BASHH balanoposthitis guideline 2025). Importantly, recurrent CANDIDAL balanitis is strongly associated with DIABETES and can be a presenting feature, so CHECK glucose/HbA1c in recurrent balanitis. Screen the causes: candidal/infective (red glans, itch, white curd-like material — commoner with diabetes, antibiotics, immunosuppression), irritant/contact dermatitis and hygiene (too little or too much), bacterial infection, STI (GUM screen if at risk), psoriasis/lichen planus, and crucially LICHEN SCLEROSUS (balanitis xerotica obliterans, BXO) — a white, atrophic, scarring change causing pathological phimosis and meatal stenosis that needs dermatology/urology involvement (potent topical steroids, sometimes circumcision) and carries a small increased penile SCC risk. Manage per cause: hygiene advice (gentle washing, drying, avoiding irritant soaps), topical antifungal ± mild steroid for candidal disease, appropriate treatment of bacterial/STI causes, and optimisation of diabetes. Refer for pathological phimosis, suspected lichen sclerosus/BXO, recurrent/refractory balanitis, or any suspicious/non-healing lesion (urology; NICE NG12: suspected cancer pathway referral for a penile mass or ulcerated lesion once an STI is excluded, a persistent lesion after STI treatment, or unexplained or persistent foreskin or glans symptoms), and consider circumcision in pathological phimosis/recurrent disease — never forcibly retracting a phimotic foreskin, examining with a chaperone offered, and treating paraphimosis as a same-day emergency. Handle an embarrassing problem sensitively, check glucose, screen for BXO, treat by cause, and safety-net. NICE NG12 applies to a persistent or suspicious penile lesion or unexplained persistent foreskin/glans symptoms.

knowledge.guideline: [1] BASHH UK national guideline on the management of balanoposthitis (2025) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE PH38 Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk (2012, updated 2017) · [4] BAD guidelines for the management of lichen sclerosus (2018) · [5] GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024)
knowledge.summary: Balanitis describes inflammation of the glans; with the foreskin involved it is balanoposthitis. It has many causes. Irritant dermatitis and skin conditions are common, and Candida is only one cause, often linked to diabetes. Recurrent episodes with a tightening foreskin in a man in his fifties need an HbA1c, swabs and STI tests as indicated, a careful look for lichen sclerosus, cause-directed treatment and urology referral for progressive phimosis. Never forcibly retract the foreskin.

points.t: BASHH [1]: irritant or allergic dermatitis (soaps, over-washing as well as poor hygiene), Candida, anaerobic or other bacterial infection, STIs including herpes and syphilis, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, psoriasis, Zoon’s balanitis, fixed drug eruption, circinate balanitis, and premalignant or malignant change. Appearance suggests a cause but is not diagnostic.

Recurrent candidal balanitis can be the first sign of diabetes. Check HbA1c in recurrent, severe or persistent cases. PH38 [3]: an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or more supports a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (confirm with a repeat test if the patient has no symptoms); 42 to 47 mmol/mol indicates high risk.

Sub-preputial swab when symptoms are severe, persistent or recurrent, there is discharge, or treatment has failed; a positive culture does not prove the cause. STI screen if at risk; HSV testing for ulcers or blisters; syphilis serology for an ulcer. Consider HIV testing in severe, persistent or atypical disease [1].

Everyone: wash gently with water, use an emollient as a soap substitute, stop soaps and perfumed products, dry well. Suspected Candida: clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily for 7 to 14 days, adding hydrocortisone 1% for a short course if very inflamed; oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose only for severe symptoms, after checking interactions (BNF). Bacterial: by clinical syndrome and local guidance. Reassess rather than keep repeating creams.

Pale or porcelain-white patches, scarring, fissuring, progressive phimosis and meatal narrowing. It scars and carries an increased risk of penile squamous cell carcinoma. Treated with an ultra-potent topical steroid through dermatology or urology, and sometimes circumcision; it needs long-term follow-up [4].

Do not forcibly retract a non-retractile foreskin. Refer to urology for pathological or progressive phimosis, recurrent balanoposthitis, meatal narrowing or suspected lichen sclerosus. Paraphimosis is a same-day emergency.

NICE NG12 [2]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for a penile mass or ulcerated lesion once an STI has been excluded, a persistent lesion after STI treatment, or unexplained or persistent symptoms affecting the foreskin or glans. A lesion hidden by a tight foreskin needs specialist assessment.

model.text: Hello Mr Okafor, I’m Dr Ahmed. What can I do for you today?

This is awkward, doctor. The end of my penis keeps getting red, sore and itchy under the foreskin, with a bit of discharge. It’s happened a few times over the last few months. And now the foreskin’s getting tight and hard to pull back. Can you sort it?
Thank you for telling me. It’s a very common problem, and there’s nothing I haven’t seen before, so please don’t feel awkward. Let’s get to the bottom of why it keeps coming back.
model.why: Normalises and puts him at ease

model.text: Okay.
When it flares, what does it look like? Any white, cheesy material, a smell, blisters, ulcers or lumps?
model.why: Features pointing to Candida, anaerobes, HSV or a lesion

model.text: Red and a bit wet. Some white stuff sometimes. No lumps or ulcers I’ve noticed.
Have you noticed any pale or white patches of skin, or the skin feeling thinner or tight at the tip? Any change in your urine stream, spraying or a weak flow?
model.why: Screens for lichen sclerosus and meatal stenosis

model.text: It’s just tight. The stream seems okay.
What do you wash with? Some people use shower gels or wash very often, which can irritate.
Just the usual shower gel.
Have you been more thirsty than usual, passing more urine, especially at night, or lost weight without trying? Any diabetes in the family, or recent antibiotics?
Not that I’ve noticed. I don’t know about the family.
I ask everyone this: is there any chance of a sexually transmitted infection, for example a new partner? And any other rashes, joint pains or sore eyes?
model.why: Non-judgemental STI risk; reactive arthritis and dermatoses

model.text: Nothing that worries me, but test for whatever you think.
I’d like to examine you. Would you like a chaperone? I won’t force the foreskin back. I’ll only look as far as it goes comfortably, then put it back.

The head of the penis and the inside of the foreskin are red and moist, with a little discharge. The foreskin only goes back part of the way. I can’t see any ulcers or lumps on what I can see, and the glands in the groin are normal. I’ll check a urine sample for sugar now and take a swab from under the foreskin.
model.why: Describes findings, notes what cannot be seen, groin nodes, urine glucose, swab

model.text: What have you been thinking it might be? Is anything worrying you?
I thought it was an infection. I’m worried it’s something serious, with the tightness.

This is called balanitis, which just means inflammation of the head of the penis. It has several causes. Soaps and scrubbing are a common one, and a yeast infection like thrush is another. Because it keeps coming back, I want to check your sugar: diabetes makes thrush much more likely and sometimes this is the first sign.
model.why: Explains balanitis, multiple causes, diabetes link

model.text: Diabetes? I’d not thought of that.
It may well not be, but it’s important to check. I’ll do a blood test called HbA1c as well as the urine test.

The tightening matters too. Repeated inflammation can scar the foreskin, and there’s a skin condition called lichen sclerosus that causes pale, tight skin. I can’t see everything today because the foreskin is tight, so I’d like a urology specialist to look at it properly. That’s not because I think it’s cancer, but anything I can’t fully see needs checking.
model.why: Progressive phimosis and possible lichen sclerosus: urology referral; honest about hidden area

model.text: Right. That’s good to know.

For now: stop the shower gel and wash just with water once a day, using a moisturising cream as a soap substitute, and dry gently. Don’t scrub. With the white material, a thrush cream such as clotrimazole twice a day for one to two weeks is sensible, with a mild steroid cream for a short time to settle the inflammation.
I’ll also offer tests for sexually transmitted infections, which we do routinely when there’s discharge. And the creams can weaken condoms, so bear that in mind.
Fine. Do I need tablets?
Not usually. The cream is the right first step. If the swab or blood test shows something else, I’ll change the plan. Does that sound all right?
Yes.

Please don’t force the foreskin back. If it ever gets stuck behind the head and won’t come forward, or you can’t pass urine, or the swelling or pain gets rapidly worse, go to A&E the same day. Come back if it isn’t clearly better in one to two weeks, or you notice a sore that won’t heal, a lump, bleeding, or a white patch. Can you tell me what we’ve agreed?
model.why: Paraphimosis and retention emergency; persistent lesion safety-net; teach-back

model.text: Water and a moisturiser instead of gel, thrush cream and the steroid cream, blood test and swabs, and you’re referring me for the tightness. Back if it’s not better in a couple of weeks, or A&E if it gets stuck.
Exactly. I’ll ring you with the blood result and see you in two weeks.

social.t: Men often delay presenting with genital symptoms. A matter-of-fact, respectful approach makes it easier to return if things change.
Discomfort and tightness can affect sex and relationships. Ask sensitively if he wishes to talk about it.

legal.t: Offer a chaperone for an intimate examination and record the offer and his decision (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).
Sexual health information is confidential. Partner notification, if needed, is handled by sexual health services with his agreement.

professional.t: Reassess, test and refer rather than issue repeated creams for a recurrent problem.
Make sure HbA1c, urine and swab results are actioned and communicated, with a clear plan if diabetes is found.

community.t: Self-referral to local sexual health clinics for STI testing, with partner notification support.
If diabetes is diagnosed, structured education and the diabetes team.

redFlags: Foreskin stuck behind the glans, retention, rapidly spreading swelling or pain: same-day emergency
Penile mass, ulcer, bleeding or non-healing lesion: NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criteria
Pale scarred skin, progressive phimosis, meatal narrowing: lichen sclerosus
ice: Concern: something serious, given the tightness

playbook.diagnosis: “This is balanitis, inflammation of the head of the penis, and the foreskin is becoming tight, which we call phimosis.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Balanitis just means the skin there is inflamed, like a rash. Soaps, yeast and some skin conditions can all cause it, so we look for the reason. Repeated inflammation can make the foreskin scar and tighten, a bit like a cuff shrinking.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was an infection and you were worried about the tightness. We’ll treat the likely cause, check for diabetes, and get the tightness looked at properly.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise; offer a chaperone; confidential STI testing.
sharedPlan: Water only, emollient soap substitute, stop shower gel, dry gently
Clotrimazole 1% twice daily for 7 to 14 days ± short hydrocortisone 1% (BASHH, BNF)
Urine glucose, HbA1c (PH38), sub-preputial swab, STI screen
Urology referral for progressive phimosis and possible lichen sclerosus
safetyNet: Foreskin stuck back, cannot pass urine, rapidly worsening swelling or pain: A&E same day
Not clearly better in 1 to 2 weeks: review
Non-healing sore, lump, bleeding or white patch: return promptly

pitfalls.intro: The trap is treating recurrent balanitis as “thrush again”. Marks go to a sensitive examination, a diabetes check, a cause-based plan and recognising that a tightening foreskin needs a specialist.

items.why: Candida is a minority cause; lichen sclerosus and malignancy are missed.
Recurrent candidal balanitis can be the first sign of diabetes.
It causes tears, scarring and paraphimosis.
items.fix: Look only as far as it retracts comfortably, then replace it.

items.why: Pathological phimosis and lichen sclerosus need urology, and a hidden glans cannot be assessed.
items.fix: Routine urology referral; NICE NG12 pathway only if criteria are met.

items.fail: Awkward or judgemental manner, especially about sexual history.
items.why: He is already embarrassed and may not return.
A stuck foreskin is an emergency.
items.fix: A&E the same day if it will not come forward or he cannot pass urine.

timeMap.d: Appearance, white patches, stream, soaps and washing, diabetes symptoms, antibiotics, STI risk, joints and eyes.
Chaperone; no forced retraction; nodes; urine glucose and swab. His fear it is serious.
Balanitis has many causes; HbA1c; lichen sclerosus and phimosis to urology; water and emollient; clotrimazole ± hydrocortisone; STI tests.
Paraphimosis or retention to A&E; review in 1 to 2 weeks; persistent lesion. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes another antifungal without examining; forces the foreskin back; no glucose check; misses the progressive phimosis; embarrassed or judgemental manner.
wordPics.pass: Examines with a chaperone offered, checks glucose, gives hygiene advice and topical treatment, screens for STI and refers the tightening foreskin to urology, with a clear safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: treats balanitis as a description needing a cause; links recurrence to a diabetes check; asks about white patches and urinary stream for lichen sclerosus; is honest that a hidden area needs specialist assessment without alarming him; explains that repeating creams is not the plan; gives paraphimosis advice; teach-back.

avoid.instead: “There are several possible causes. Let’s test and treat the most likely one, and look again if it doesn’t settle.”
avoid.why: BASHH: Candida is a minority cause; repeated empirical treatment misses lichen sclerosus and malignancy.

avoid.dont: “Pull it back so I can see.”
avoid.instead: “I’ll only look as far as it goes comfortably.”
avoid.why: Forced retraction causes tears, scarring and paraphimosis.

avoid.dont: “Could be cancer, I’ll refer you urgently.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t see everything under the tight foreskin, so a specialist should look.”
avoid.why: Accurate, calm explanation; NICE NG12 criteria are applied only if met.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] BASHH UK national guideline on the management of balanoposthitis (2025) · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE PH38 Type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk (2012, updated 2017) · [4] BAD guidelines for the management of lichen sclerosus (2018) · [5] GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Balanitis describes inflammation of the glans; with the foreskin involved it is balanoposthitis. It has many causes. Irritant dermatitis and skin conditions are common, and Candida is only one cause, often linked to diabetes. Recurrent episodes with a tightening foreskin in a man in his fifties need an HbA1c, swabs and STI tests as indicated, a careful look for lichen sclerosus, cause-directed treatment and urology referral for progressive phimosis. Never forcibly retract the foreskin.

points.t: BASHH [1]: irritant or allergic dermatitis (soaps, over-washing as well as poor hygiene), Candida, anaerobic or other bacterial infection, STIs including herpes and syphilis, lichen sclerosus, lichen planus, psoriasis, Zoon’s balanitis, fixed drug eruption, circinate balanitis, and premalignant or malignant change. Appearance suggests a cause but is not diagnostic.

Recurrent candidal balanitis can be the first sign of diabetes. Check HbA1c in recurrent, severe or persistent cases. PH38 [3]: an HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or more supports a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes (confirm with a repeat test if the patient has no symptoms); 42 to 47 mmol/mol indicates high risk.

Sub-preputial swab when symptoms are severe, persistent or recurrent, there is discharge, or treatment has failed; a positive culture does not prove the cause. STI screen if at risk; HSV testing for ulcers or blisters; syphilis serology for an ulcer. Consider HIV testing in severe, persistent or atypical disease [1].

Everyone: wash gently with water, use an emollient as a soap substitute, stop soaps and perfumed products, dry well. Suspected Candida: clotrimazole 1% cream twice daily for 7 to 14 days, adding hydrocortisone 1% for a short course if very inflamed; oral fluconazole 150 mg single dose only for severe symptoms, after checking interactions (BNF). Bacterial: by clinical syndrome and local guidance. Reassess rather than keep repeating creams.

Pale or porcelain-white patches, scarring, fissuring, progressive phimosis and meatal narrowing. It scars and carries an increased risk of penile squamous cell carcinoma. Treated with an ultra-potent topical steroid through dermatology or urology, and sometimes circumcision; it needs long-term follow-up [4].

Do not forcibly retract a non-retractile foreskin. Refer to urology for pathological or progressive phimosis, recurrent balanoposthitis, meatal narrowing or suspected lichen sclerosus. Paraphimosis is a same-day emergency.

NICE NG12 [2]: consider a suspected cancer pathway referral for a penile mass or ulcerated lesion once an STI has been excluded, a persistent lesion after STI treatment, or unexplained or persistent symptoms affecting the foreskin or glans. A lesion hidden by a tight foreskin needs specialist assessment.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; normalised an embarrassing problem early.
Washing habits, embarrassment, sexual health asked non-judgementally.
Picked up recurrence as a diabetes cue and the tightening foreskin as a sign needing referral.
Idea (infection), concern (something serious with the tightness), expectation (a cure).
Offered a chaperone; examined without forcible retraction; groin nodes; urine glucose, swab, HbA1c, STI screen.
Candidal, irritant, bacterial, STI, lichen sclerosus, other dermatoses and premalignant change.
Screened for lumps, ulcers, white patches, urinary stream change and paraphimosis risk; NICE NG12 awareness.
Explained balanitis as a description with several causes, and developing phimosis.
Water and emollient hygiene; clotrimazole with short hydrocortisone; reassess rather than repeat; urology referral for progressive phimosis.
Diabetes tested and linked to recurrence; STI tests; condom advice.
Paraphimosis and retention to A&E; review if not better in 1 to 2 weeks; non-healing sore, lump or white patch; teach-back.

social.t: Men often delay presenting with genital symptoms. A matter-of-fact, respectful approach makes it easier to return if things change.
Discomfort and tightness can affect sex and relationships. Ask sensitively if he wishes to talk about it.

legal.t: Offer a chaperone for an intimate examination and record the offer and his decision (GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones, 2024).
Sexual health information is confidential. Partner notification, if needed, is handled by sexual health services with his agreement.

professional.t: Reassess, test and refer rather than issue repeated creams for a recurrent problem.
Make sure HbA1c, urine and swab results are actioned and communicated, with a clear plan if diabetes is found.

community.t: Self-referral to local sexual health clinics for STI testing, with partner notification support.
If diabetes is diagnosed, structured education and the diabetes team.

redFlags: Foreskin stuck behind the glans, retention, rapidly spreading swelling or pain: same-day emergency
Penile mass, ulcer, bleeding or non-healing lesion: NICE NG12 suspected cancer pathway criteria
Pale scarred skin, progressive phimosis, meatal narrowing: lichen sclerosus
ice: Concern: something serious, given the tightness

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is balanitis, inflammation of the head of the penis, and the foreskin is becoming tight, which we call phimosis.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Balanitis just means the skin there is inflamed, like a rash. Soaps, yeast and some skin conditions can all cause it, so we look for the reason. Repeated inflammation can make the foreskin scar and tighten, a bit like a cuff shrinking.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought it was an infection and you were worried about the tightness. We’ll treat the likely cause, check for diabetes, and get the tightness looked at properly.”
management.psychosocial: Normalise; offer a chaperone; confidential STI testing.
sharedPlan: Water only, emollient soap substitute, stop shower gel, dry gently
Clotrimazole 1% twice daily for 7 to 14 days ± short hydrocortisone 1% (BASHH, BNF)
Urine glucose, HbA1c (PH38), sub-preputial swab, STI screen
Urology referral for progressive phimosis and possible lichen sclerosus
safetyNet: Foreskin stuck back, cannot pass urine, rapidly worsening swelling or pain: A&E same day
Not clearly better in 1 to 2 weeks: review
Non-healing sore, lump, bleeding or white patch: return promptly

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is treating recurrent balanitis as “thrush again”. Marks go to a sensitive examination, a diabetes check, a cause-based plan and recognising that a tightening foreskin needs a specialist.

items.why: Candida is a minority cause; lichen sclerosus and malignancy are missed.
Recurrent candidal balanitis can be the first sign of diabetes.
It causes tears, scarring and paraphimosis.
items.fix: Look only as far as it retracts comfortably, then replace it.

items.why: Pathological phimosis and lichen sclerosus need urology, and a hidden glans cannot be assessed.
items.fix: Routine urology referral; NICE NG12 pathway only if criteria are met.

items.fail: Awkward or judgemental manner, especially about sexual history.
items.why: He is already embarrassed and may not return.
A stuck foreskin is an emergency.
items.fix: A&E the same day if it will not come forward or he cannot pass urine.
